newsitem.title: USA: Ahmanson bids $6 billion for Great Western.
newsitem.headline: Ahmanson bids $6 billion for Great Western.

text.p: H.F. Ahmanson & Co. said Tuesday it offered to buy Great Western Financial Corp. for $6 billion in stock in a deal that would combine the nation's two largest savings and loans companies.
Ahmanson, the nation's largest thrift, said it offered to swap 1.05 of its shares for each share of Great Western, the country's second-largest savings and loan holding company.

A combination of the two companies, which are both based in the Los Angeles area, would create a powerhouse with $93 billion in assets and be the latest merger among thrifts in an industry shakeout in California.
Ahmanson said its bid valued Great Western at a premium of about 24 percent over the stock's closing price Friday.

But investors were betting that another bidder might emerge for Great Western or that Ahmanson would have to raise its offer, takeover specialists said. They said Great Western was probably shopping for an investment banker to advise it and may be trying to line up a "white knight" to rescue it from Ahmanson.
Great Western stock jumped $10.50 to $44.75 and Ahmanson added $4.25 to $44.75, both in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
Great Western Financial President John Maher said his company was reviewing the offer.
"Great Western will respond to H.F. Ahmanson when it has had an opportunity to fully review and evaluate this proposal with its board of directors and advisors," he said.

Great Western, based in Chatsworth, Calif., has about 14,300 employees and 1,150 offices, mostly in California and Florida. Ahmanson, based in Irwindale, owns several savings banks, including two big thrifts in New York state, and has about 450 branch offices.
Ahmanson's announcement had all the earmarks of a hostile bid, though it was not yet clear that Great Western had decided to resist.
Ahmanson's Chairman Charles Rinehart said on CNBC that he had spoken to Great Western's Maher on Monday night and that Maher had been surprised to hear of the bid.
Wall Street analysts said some branch closings were likely if a deal was completed and that the merged company would be a powerful force in its main markets in California and Florida.
"This is a very positive transaction for Ahmanson in that elimination of overlapping branches would drive considerable cost savings," said Morgan Stanley & Co. analyst Kenneth Posner.
Ahmanson said the merger would result in $400 million in savings a year.
Some takeover traders were betting that Washington Mutual Savings Bank would emerge as Great Western's white knight.
In the recent wave of thrift mergers on the West Coast, Washington Mutual has made several acquisitions and San Francisco-based First Nationwide Holdings Inc. has acquired Cal Fed Bancorp.
Ahmanson said the expected cost-savings, along with stock repurchases, would boost its earnings per share this year and the next two years.
It added that the deal would be accounted for as a purchase and would be tax-free. The transaction would be subject to approval by both companies' boards and regulators.
One takeover specialist said he antitrust issues would not be a major stumbling block to a Ahmanson-Great Western deal.

Ahmanson also said it would nominate three people to Great Western's board -- Lawrence Del Santo, chairman of the Vons Cos., Robert Gelber, former partner of the law firm Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher, and Wolfgang Schoellkopf, former vice chairman of First Fidelity Bancorp.
